examples: Whether your education is high or low, effort is indispensable.
Rain or snow, the tournament will be held as scheduled.
Rich or poor, everyone is equal under the law.
Whatever it is, please consult me first.
Wherever she goes, she makes friends right away.
Whatever the result, I intend to accept it.
fields.explain:
Placed after a noun; does not attach directly to an adjective/verb (nominalize if needed).
Formal style, used in essays, speeches, regulations, and official announcements.
であれ is usually repeated twice with a pair N1・N2; with a question word, only one であれ is needed.
The second clause is usually a general judgment, a policy, a principle, or a strong volition.
Can be combined with たとえ to add the nuance of "even if".

• Expresses "whether it is A or B, the conclusion/position does not change". Emphasizes that the stance is unchanging.
• With 疑問詞 + であれ, it means "no matter …", with a broad scope (covering every possibility).
• Often pairs two nouns that are opposites/extremes to create a strong contrast: 高い⇔低い, 雨⇔雪, 金持ち⇔貧乏…
• The nuance is stiff and rule-like or principled; the second clause is often a general judgment/direction, and it is rarely used for private, casual matters.
• Morphologically, であれ comes from the imperative form of である, but in this pattern it carries no meaning of command; it expresses the supposition "even if it is".
fields.notes:
• When you need to attach it to an adjective/verb, use a noun denoting a type/matter: 忙しい人であれ (busy person); 必要であれ is incorrect; instead: 必要な場合であれ.
• In spoken language, it is often replaced with でも/にせよ to sound more natural.
• In tone, であれ carries a sense of "no exceptions", which suits expressing policies and rules.
mistakes: Wrong part of speech: attaching it directly to an i-adj/na-adj/verb. You need to nominalize: 忙しいときであれ / 重要な案件であれ.
Lack of parallelism when using a pair: N1 and N2 must belong to the same category and be balanced: 正しいであれ間違いであれ (correct), 正しいであれ急ぐであれ (incorrect).
Using it in an overly casual context makes the sentence sound forced. JLPT N1 often tests the formal nuance of であれ compared with でも.
Confusion with にせよ: both are correct in many sentences, but exam questions often ask you to choose the pattern that fits the style; in normative texts, であれ is preferred.
Trap with question words: 何であれ (correct), 何でもであれ (incorrect because the functions overlap).

examples: Even a child can understand this explanation.
He is so busy that he doesn't even have time for lunch.
It is a problem that even experts are at a loss over.
Even the critics praised her singing voice.
I was so tired that I didn't even dream last night.
He doesn't even know something that basic? Can't he even write his own name correctly?
fields.explain:
Used to heighten the sense of surprise/the unexpected; it can be used in both affirmative and negative sentences.
In written language/speeches, "ですら" is more formal than "さえ/でさえ".
If you need to keep a case particle, use "N＋助詞＋すら" (夢にすら,彼とすら…).

• Emphasizes the degree of surprise: even the target at the lower edge/beyond expectations does (not) …
• "ですら" has a formal nuance; "すら/でさえ/さえ" are more commonly used.
• When a case particle (に/と/から…) is needed, "ですら" cannot be inserted; use "N＋助詞＋すら".
fields.notes:
• In strong negation, it can go with まったく／全然: 彼は挨拶すらしない.
• Avoid doubling particles: × 子どもにですら → either 子どもですら (no need for に), or 子どもにすら.
mistakes: Wrong particle position: × 彼ですらに → correct: 彼にすら.
Using "ですら" right after a case particle: × 学校にですら → use 学校にすら or 学校ですら (depending on the meaning).
Confusing the nuance with "まで": "まで" means to the extent of/even, but does not always carry the sense of surprise that "すら" does.

rows: Most common; has many structural variants
<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>さえあれば<ruby>生<rt>い</rt></ruby>きられる
Used when "に/と/から…" is needed

examples: Because it is the first day of the long holiday, the airport is crowded everywhere.
With a famous shop closing down, a long line had formed since morning.
Since it was the first sunny day in a long time, the park was bustling with families.
Because it is the last day of the sale, the store is filled with excitement.
With a popular actor visiting Japan, security around the venue was tightened.
fields.explain:
The second clause is an objective result/phenomenon; avoid using the speaker's command/volition.
Presents the "special/rare" nature of the cause:連休、初雪、有名人来訪…
Usually used with the present tense or the past progressive (～ている/～ていた).

• A "special/noteworthy" reason leads to a natural, observed result.
• A narrative/objective tone; not suitable for stating the speaker's volition/request.
• Often used in news, articles, and commentary on social phenomena.
fields.notes:
• N2. Very common in newspaper reading passages; recognize it by a "special" noun + とあって.
• Placed at the beginning of a sentence; rarely comes after another subordinate clause.
• Not used with the speaker's direct request/desire: × とあって、手伝ってください。
mistakes: Using it for the speaker's volition: × とあって、早く帰ろうと思う → use ので/ため instead.
Confusion with ～だけあって (evaluation) or ～とあれば (condition). Pay attention to the second clause.
A cause that is not "special" makes the sentence awkward; choose a cause that stands out.

<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>とあれば<ruby>協力<rt>きょうりょく</rt></ruby>する

<ruby>一流<rt>いちりゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>店<rt>てん</rt></ruby>だけあって<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い
Neutral; does not need to be "special"
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>のため<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>

examples: Both the scenery and the air here are truly wonderful.
This restaurant leaves nothing to be desired, in both taste and price.
In both looks and personality, he is flawless.
That athlete is first-class in both speed and stamina.
In both performance and design, this computer is great value for money.
Both his attitude and the way he talks are a bit rude.
fields.explain:
Used to give an "overall evaluation" based on two representative points.
Not used with commands, invitations, or intentions. It mainly ends in descriptive/evaluative narrative sentences.
Usually used with nouns; rarely used directly with adjectives/verbs. Do not confuse it with "Vるといい" (the wish "if only").
Suitable for written language, commentary, reviews, and concise praise/criticism.

- Meaning: "Both N1 and N2 (from whichever aspect you look at it)…". Used to sum up the value/impression of a target based on two representative features.
- Nuance: Describes a subjective evaluation, usually positive (praise), sometimes negative (criticism). Not used for the speaker's requests/volition.
- The subject is usually the target being evaluated; N1 and N2 are "representative aspects" of that target.
fields.notes:
• When listing more than 2 aspects, the sentence may become heavy; usually only 2 representative ones are chosen.
• Suitable for opening the first sentence of an evaluative paragraph: "立地といい設備といい、…"
• Can be used for criticism: "雨といい風といい、最悪の天気だ"。
mistakes: Confusion with "Vるといい(ね)": completely different meaning.
Using it to make a request/suggestion: Not appropriate.
Attaching it directly to a verb/adjective without nominalization: Unnatural.
JLPT: the trap of choosing "AやB" (simple listing) instead of "AといいBといい" (overall evaluation).

<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>といい<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>といい、<ruby>最高<rt>さいこう</rt></ruby>
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>にしても<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>にしても<ruby>楽<rt>たの</rt></ruby>しめる

<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>や<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby>
Completely different in meaning and usage
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>くなるといいね

fields.connection: Vる / N / Quantity + というところだ
examples: The preparations are about 80% done.
We'll probably arrive at around 3 p.m.
This year's growth rate is roughly a 5% increase.
My Japanese is at about an intermediate level.
For now, the damage can be said to be minor.
Even if we finish today, it will only be about half.
fields.explain:
Used when summing up/estimating after weighing the facts; it has a sense of "putting it briefly".
Often accompanied by だろう／でしょう to soften the statement.
Not used for commands/suggestions; it is a narrative sentence of evaluation.

- Meaning: "About…, roughly…, around … at most". Expresses an estimate/evaluation that sums things up at the point in time of speaking.
- Nuance: Objective, somewhat formal; often used in reports, news, and expert assessments. Depending on the context, it may imply "at most/not very high".
- Often accompanied by quantifying expressions (割, パーセント, 時間, 人, 点…) or levels (初級/中級/平均的…).
fields.notes:
• Suitable when you need to "anchor" a representative number/level of evaluation, so that it is not taken as an exact value.
• To reduce the nuance of certainty, preferably end with でしょう/だろう or add おそらく/たぶん.
• When assessing your own ability/level, it gives a modest, polite tone in self-introductions.
mistakes: Using it as an absolutely exact figure: Incorrect; it is an estimate.
Confusion with ところ (in the middle of, about to, just did): というところだ is completely different.
Using it in a command/suggestion: Does not fit its function.
JLPT: the trap of choosing せいぜい when the context is neutral (せいぜい has the nuance of "at most").

rows: せいぜい<ruby>半分<rt>はんぶん</rt></ruby>

examples: Sales have recovered, but they are still only about 70% of pre-COVID levels.
At most, I get about two days off a month.
The preparation period is only about a week, which can hardly be called enough.
The passing line is around 60 points.
As for my mountain-climbing experience, I've only joined a trial tour once.
fields.explain:
Suitable for cautious statements that avoid absolutes; fits written language/presentations.
Not used for boasting/emphasizing superiority; the main nuance is "modest, limited".
Often used to end a sentence giving an assessment of figures, degree, or scope.

• Expresses an approximate degree or an upper limit, "at most, only this much", with a modest/limiting nuance.
• Often accompanied by limiting words such as せいぜい、多くても、せめて to emphasize the ceiling.
• Pragmatics: More formal than くらい/ぐらい; often used in reports and objective assessments.
fields.notes:
• Works well in academic writing/reports: an open conclusion that leaves a margin of error.
• When talking about your personal experience/qualifications, it helps avoid boasting: "勉強したといったところだ"。
• Placed at the end of a sentence to keep the tone soft and polite while still precise.
mistakes: Using it to exaggerate has the wrong nuance: ×最高で100人も来るといったところだ.
Confusion with くらい: JLPT often asks you to choose the "modest" pattern → prefer といったところだ.
Missing the "upper limit" context: if the meaning is "at least", do not use といったところだ.

rows: Neutral, more spoken; does not imply "at most".
<ruby>30人<rt>さんじゅうにん</rt></ruby>ぐらい<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る。
Strong on degree; can be used to exaggerate.
<ruby>息<rt>いき</rt></ruby>ができないほど<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い。
Spoken; can be combined: せいぜい<ruby>三回<rt>さんかい</rt></ruby>といったところだ。
せいぜい<ruby>二<rt>に</rt></ruby><ruby>千<rt>せん</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>。

examples: It's unbearably cold. I can't manage without heating.
His room is filthy beyond words.
The rush-hour commuter crowds are indescribable.
My boss is unbelievably fickle.
The fees are outrageously high.
fields.explain:
Leans toward complaint/irritation more than praise.
Spoken language; sounds rather strong and can be crude if used with strangers/in polite situations.
Placed before a concluding/justifying clause: …ので/から/も無理はない…
Goes easily with nouns of states:混みよう・暑さ・痛み・迷惑・恥ずかしさ…

- Expresses an extremely high degree, "very/beyond words", usually with negative emotions (irritation, weariness). "ありはしない" is the emphatic negation of ある → a colloquial nuance, somewhat stiff/strong and full of emotion.
• Focuses on the speaker's subjective impression.
• Suitable for complaining, criticizing, and lamenting; rarely used in formal, objective writing.
• Hyperbolic: it does not mean "there is none", but "too much to put into words".
fields.notes:
• "ありはしない" = "ありはしない(=全くないわけではない, emphasizes negation)" is used to exaggerate the degree.
• Often stands as an independent sentence of exclamation, followed by a sentence of explanation.
• Rarely used for praise, but possible: ありがたさといったらありはしない (still sounds exaggerated/unusual).
mistakes: Using it directly with the dictionary form of a verb: unnatural. You should nominalize the phenomenon. Incorrect) 驚くといったらありはしない → Correct) 驚きといったらありはしない.
Confusing the nuance: exam questions often ask you to distinguish といったらない (neutral) vs ありはしない (negative/colloquial).
Using it in formal writing: not appropriate; choose といったらない/極めて/非常に.
Meaningless double negation: "〜ないといったらありはしない" easily muddles the meaning → avoid it.

examples: Day and night alike, the ambulance sirens never stop.
The classroom is covered in dust, the floor and the desks alike.
Children and adults alike are hooked on this anime.
I got mud all over, my face and hands alike.
Weekdays and weekends alike, the library is crowded.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize "no exclusions" over a broad scope, with repetition or simultaneity.
The second clause is not a direct volition/command. Avoid: ×子どもといわず大人といわず、集まりなさい。
Most natural with concrete nouns/opposing pairs; be careful with abstract nouns.

• Emphasizes a broad scope: "without excluding/distinguishing … or …, everything is …".
• Often used with natural pairs: 昼／夜, 老人／子供, 左／右, 内／外, 表／裏…
• Strong nuance, somewhat written; the second clause is usually a lasting state, universality, or a pervasive degree (～だらけ、～まみれ、～が続く…).
fields.notes:
• Rhetorically effective when describing "everywhere/all at once": it easily creates rhythm and emphasis.
• Combines well with degree words "だらけ／まみれ／いっぱい／あふれる／鳴りやまない／絶えない".
• Three items can be used for intensification (rare): 昼といわず夜といわず朝といわず… but avoid being long-winded.
mistakes: Using it with a command/volition → unnatural.
Confusion with ～を問わず in the context of signs/regulations: JLPT usually requires choosing the formal pattern → use ～を問わず.
Listing nouns that are asymmetrical/not in the same semantic field makes the sentence awkward.

rows: Formal; does not emphasize pervasiveness like といわず～といわず.
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby><ruby>可<rt>か</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>にかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>。
Only lists illustrations; does not cover the whole.
<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>ない。

fields.meaning: To be considered…, to be regarded as…
fields.connection: [sentence/clause] + とされる とされている / N
examples: This region is said to have a high risk of earthquakes.
He is regarded as the leading authority in the field of AI.
This temple is considered the oldest in Japan.
Vitamin D is considered important for bone health.
According to reports, a man believed to be the culprit has been arrested.
This custom has been said to date back to the Edo period.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to stay neutral and not make an absolute claim; suitable for reports, theses, and news.
Add a source/criterion to clarify the basis:一般には／法律上は／統計的には／専門家の間では + 〜とされる.
Not used for very personal opinions; when subjective, と思う／と考える is more appropriate.

• Expresses an evaluation/standard/view accepted by many people or by experts: "is considered/is said to be".
• Objective nuance with no clear agent; the speaker takes no personal responsibility for the evaluation.
• Difference in degree:

- とされる: a common conclusion/designation (usually in written, academic, legal, and journalistic language).

- とされている: a general assessment that currently holds, slightly softer.

• Can be accompanied by a source: 専門家によって／法律上／一般には + 〜とされる.
fields.notes:
• In newspaper headlines, the subject is often omitted: 「世界最古とされる洞窟を発見」 → "Cave considered the oldest in the world discovered".
• In academic writing, combine with 出典/調査名 to increase credibility: 「〜とされる（Smith, 2021）」.
• The negative form is rare: 〜とはされない（"is not considered"） when excluding something in legal contexts/regulations.
mistakes: Confusing the nuance: とされる ≠ と言われている. JLPT questions often test objectivity; choose とされる when the style is formal/academic.
Forgetting ている: When emphasizing a lasting general state → prefer とされている.
Using it for a personal opinion → wrong style. For personal views, use と思う／と考える.
Modifier: N + とされる + N is a journalistic structure; do not insert だ before とされる in a modifier.
